config.system_prompt:
You are a strategy analyst investigating an opportunity for a manufacturer. Use these tools:
read_brief {} : read the company, the question and your budgets.
frame_problem {"objective":"...","constraints":["..."],"alternatives":["..."]} : state the real objective and the options, including ones the question did not suggest. Accepted once.
search_evidence {"query":"..."} : keyword search of the evidence. Uses one search.
challenge_theory {"theory_id":"T1","query":"..."} : search for evidence that could prove a theory wrong. Uses one search.
read_source {"id":"..."} : read a result found by search.
add_theory {"claim":"...","who_benefits":"...","why_behaviour_changes":"...","how_value_is_captured":"...","assumptions":["..."],"predictions":["..."]} : add one causal theory of value. Returns its id.
assess_evidence {"theory_id":"T1","evidence_id":"...","direction":"supports or contradicts or neutral","quote":"exact words from the source","evidence_kind":"company_assertion or customer_observation or independent_study or regulation or analogy or market_fact","does_not_show":"what this evidence cannot establish"} : say how evidence bears on a theory, honestly. Use neutral if it does neither.
propose_test {"name":"...","theories":["T1","T2"],"method":"...","sample":"...","measure":"...","prediction_by_theory":{"T1":"...","T2":"..."},"decision_rule":"...","cost_eur":N,"weeks":N} : design an experiment where the theories predict different results.
revise_theory {"theory_id":"T1","status":"kept or revised or rejected","reason":"...","new_claim":"the changed claim, or none","evidence_ids":["..."]} : update a theory after new evidence.
finish {"recommendation":"...","target_customer":"...","value_proposition":"...","favoured_theory":"T1","next_action":"...","uncertainty":"...","would_change_if":["..."],"evidence_ids":["..."]} : end the investigation.

Reply with one JSON object: {"name": "<tool>", "arguments": {...}}. A user turn that starts with "Tool result:" is the output of your call. End by calling finish.

Work like a scientist, not a consultant.
1. read_brief, then frame_problem. List at least three alternatives, including no expansion and options the question did not suggest.
2. Search before you theorise. Find out what the company already sells to individual buyers, and do not assume. Read at least three sources.
3. add_theory at least twice, and a third time if you have a different cause. A theory is a causal explanation of why people behave as they do, not advice. Do not write "the company should". Each theory needs a different cause: who benefits, why they would change behaviour, how the manufacturer captures value. Give assumptions, and predictions someone could measure.
For example, from eyewear: "People treat glasses as a medical necessity. If they came to see them as fashion, they would own several pairs, so a maker that controls design and retail could earn premium prices." A rival theory would name a different cause.
4. assess_evidence for every theory, quoting the source's exact words. Say what kind of evidence it is and what it cannot show. A company's own claim is not proof of demand. Use challenge_theory to look for evidence that could prove your favoured theory wrong. If you find nothing against it, say so. Never force a contradiction.
5. propose_test: an affordable experiment where the theories predict different results, with a decision rule that has a threshold.
6. If new evidence arrives, read it and use revise_theory.
7. finish. Say what you recommend, the next action, what is uncertain, and what would change your mind.

Every number or fact you present as observed must come from a source you read. Numbers you propose, such as a test's sample, budget, duration, threshold or an estimate, are allowed when you label them as proposed or estimated. Your theories are hypotheses, not facts. Results marked SIMULATED are not real demand, so never cite one in finish.

A controller opens the tools for each stage, and each tool result lists them. Before you finish you will also use:
decline_test {"reason":"..."} : say why more information is not worth its cost here, instead of proposing a test.
state_position {"favoured_theory":"T1","recommendation":"...","beliefs":{"T1":"likely","T2":"uncertain"}} : say what you believe now, rating each theory very unlikely, unlikely, uncertain, likely or very likely. finish then also takes "beliefs".
A SIMULATED result is a what-if exercise. Reason as if it were real, and say what it would mean for your theories. A result can change nothing. Still keep it out of the evidence you cite.

position.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer proposition yet. Run the proposed small-scale test (X1) before any product or channel investment, and treat the compact-machine idea as unproven. T1 is the one worth testing because it is the only theory with a direct, measurable buyer behaviour. The evidence so far is thin: three news and company sources, none of which measures willingness to buy.

frame.objective: Decide whether Rieter should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its industrial short-staple spinning business, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. Judge the question on public evidence only, and say what cannot be established without company data.
constraints: Outside analyst working from public sources only; no contact with the company and no knowledge of its intentions.
Test budget EUR 20,000 and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures.
8 searches in total, 7 remaining; each source must be read before it is cited.
Core business is B2B: systems, components and after-sales for spinning mills with more than 3,000 mill customers; Barmag (man-made fibre equipment) owned since February 2026.
Contract values, margins by segment, and any existing direct-to-consumer activity may not be public.
Any consumer proposition must not damage relationships with industrial mill customers who are the core buyers.
alternatives: A. No expansion: keep the industrial model and focus capital on core systems, components, after-sales and the Barmag integration.
B. Product redesign: adapt spinning or winding technology into a smaller, lower-cost machine for a consumer or small-scale use case, sold to a different buyer.
C. Different route to buyers: keep the product but sell or service through distributors, online channels or training partnerships reaching hobbyists, craft producers or small workshops.

D. Different customer group with a service model: serve artisan or heritage yarn producers, educational institutions or home textile makers through rental, leasing or training rather than machine sales.
E. Consumer-facing know-how or fibre-quality service: sell spinning process knowledge, data or quality services directly to end users or brands, without selling machines to consumers.
F. Partnership or licensing: license technology or co-develop with a consumer-facing maker, keeping Rieter's B2B position intact.

T1.claim: Small fibre mills have unmet demand for capacity because industrial machines are sized for large volumes. A compact, lower-cost spinning line sold to small craft and farm mills would win orders at a premium, because owners would pay for capacity they cannot otherwise get.
T1.who_benefits: Small fibre mills, craft yarn producers and fibre farms that cannot buy or run industrial equipment, and a machine maker able to sell a smaller line.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Mini mills run 6 to 12 spindles while industrial equipment runs 240, and the Maine mills report waitlists of at least six months, so buyers who now wait or send fibre out may switch to owning their own capacity if a machine suits their scale and budget.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Rieter sells a compact machine line, or a reduced configuration of existing spinning equipment, for a price per spindle higher than the industrial per-unit cost, plus spares and service.
assumptions: Waitlists reflect a shortage of mill capacity rather than a shortage of fibre or customers.
Small mills will pay enough for a compact machine to cover its development and sales cost.
The compact machine can be built from existing Rieter parts without a large fixed development cost.
Buyers in the US and Europe share the same small-scale demand pattern.
predictions: Mills with waitlists will report willingness to buy owned machines at a stated price within a 12-week survey.
Mills that send fibre out will convert to owned equipment at a measurable rate when a compact option is offered.
Orders will cluster among mills that already process to yarn, not among hobby spinners.
T1.first_claim: Small fibre mills have unmet demand for capacity because industrial machines are sized for large volumes. A compact, lower-cost spinning line sold to small craft and farm mills would win orders at a premium, because owners would pay for capacity they cannot otherwise get.

T2.claim: The waitlists reflect a shortage of skilled operators, training and fibre supply rather than machine capacity. Small mills would pay for know-how, process setup and training more readily than for hardware, so a service layer would capture value where a machine sale would not.
T2.who_benefits: Small mills and craft producers that lack trained spinners, and a supplier able to sell training, setup and process services alongside existing equipment.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: A mill with a six-month waitlist may be limited by its staff and raw fibre rather than its machines. Adding a machine would not relieve that limit, so the owner would buy help with process and skills first.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Rieter or a partner sells training courses, process set-up, quality advice or certification support priced per day or per project, with machine sales as a later step.
assumptions: Mills with waitlists are constrained by people or fibre, not by machine count.
Owners will pay for training and process support when they cannot hire experienced spinners.
A service sold to small mills can be delivered without large fixed cost.
predictions: Mills with waitlists will name staffing or fibre supply as their main constraint more often than machine count.
Mills offered training will take up the offer at a higher rate than mills offered a machine.
Demand for a service will show a different buyer profile from demand for machines, with more hobby and new-entrant buyers.

X1.name: Compact capacity versus training offer, small fibre mills
X1.method: Survey of small fibre and yarn mills, then a randomised offer of two priced options: a compact owned spinning line or a training and process set-up package. The offer is a refundable deposit or letter of intent, not a sale. Also record each mill's main stated constraint: machine capacity, staff, or fibre supply.
X1.sample: Proposed: 60 small mills and craft yarn producers, half in Maine or New England and half in Europe, drawn from fibre-festival and mill association lists. Mills that process to yarn and have waitlists are oversampled. Hobby spinners are excluded from the main count and reported separately.
X1.measure: Share of mills that take up each offer with a refundable deposit; stated primary constraint (capacity, staff, fibre); and the price band at which the compact machine is taken up.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Owned compact-machine deposits exceed training-package deposits, and capacity is the most common stated constraint among waitlisted mills.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Training-package deposits match or exceed machine deposits, and staffing or fibre supply is the most common stated constraint among waitlisted mills.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: continue on T1 only if at least 20% of waitlisted mills take a machine deposit, machine deposits exceed training deposits by at least 10 percentage points, and capacity is named by more mills than staff. If training deposits match or exceed machine deposits, or staffing is named most often, reject T1 and pursue the service route. If neither threshold is met, the result is inconclusive and no investment decision is made.

revisions.reason: The result is SIMULATED and states that no study was conducted, so it is a what-if and not evidence. Even if it were real, it would bear on a narrow mechanism in a recruited hobby group (skill barrier changing deposits) and would not show the machine can be built at a price buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Rieter's business. It does not change my belief about T2. T2 stays kept as a rival that the X1 test would check. The real sources listed are the only ones relied on.

SYN-RIETER-UPDATE is SIMULATED and states that no study was conducted. If it were real, it would show only that, in a recruited hobby group, paid instructor onboarding drew more refundable deposits (72 of 400) than a manual alone (32 of 400). That would bear on T2's skill-barrier mechanism, and would not show a compact machine can be built at a price buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Rieter's business. It is a what-if, so I do not treat it as evidence and I do not change my belief about T2 or T1 on it. It is excluded from the finish.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer proposition now. The evidence I could read is too thin to justify investment. Keep the industrial model as the base, and run a small, low-cost test (X1, proposed at EUR 18,000 over 12 weeks, an estimate) before any product redesign, distributor route or service launch. If the test is not run, the default is no expansion.
final.target_customer: Small fibre and yarn mills, and possibly part-time craft producers. Public evidence suggests small mills are a niche. This is not established for Rieter's market.
final.value_proposition: Untested. Two candidates: a compact spinning line sold to small mills (T1), or training and set-up support sold alongside existing equipment (T2). Neither has measured willingness to pay.
final.next_action: Run test X1, or a cheaper version, with the decision rule set beforehand: continue on T1 only if at least 20% of waitlisted mills take a machine deposit, machine deposits exceed training deposits by at least 10 points, and capacity is named more often than staff. First obtain company data on existing consumer or small-customer sales and segment margins.
final.uncertainty: Large. I found no public evidence that Rieter sells to individual buyers, and could not confirm distributor or licence routes. Market evidence is one Maine news report on four mills plus one mill owner's remark. Nothing measures willingness to pay, market size or unit cost. Contract values and margins are unknown.
would_change_if: Evidence Rieter already sells compact or small-customer equipment to individuals.
Test X1 shows machine deposits below 20%, or training matching or beating machine deposits, or staffing named most often.
Public data showing the small-mill market is too small to cover a compact line's development cost.
Company data showing a compact line could reuse existing parts at low fixed cost.
Evidence that waitlists are caused by fibre supply rather than machine capacity.

result.title: Simulated mini-spinning-machine onboarding offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 32 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: The result is SIMULATED and states that no study was conducted, so it is a what-if and not evidence. Even if it were real, it would bear on a narrow mechanism in a recruited hobby group (skill barrier changing deposits) and would not show the machine can be built at a price buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Rieter's business. It does not change my belief about T2 or T1 and is not cited. T2 stays kept as a rival that the X1 test would check.

If the test is not run, the default is no expansion.

tool_result.title: Simulated mini-spinning-machine onboarding offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 32 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
